prompt:
Write 12 short claim log entries (one to three sentences each) by an auto insurance adjuster for a low-speed head-on collision claim, in time order. Injury: neck and back strain. The claimant is not represented by a lawyer. Start each entry on a new line with 'Entry 1:', 'Entry 2:' and so on. No names, dates or amounts. (Internal reference C-1329; do not mention it.) Work these facts into the text naturally, in your own words, without listing them:
- The injury does not fit the crash: the impact was very light, yet the claimed injury is severe.
- Treatment followed a usual course and tapered off as the patient improved.
- No earlier injury to the same body area is known.
- Nothing independent confirms the accident: no witnesses, no photos and no other report.
- The damage does not match the story: the dents are on another side and at another height than the described impact.
- The claimant told the same account in every conversation.
- The police and witnesses confirm the claimant was in the vehicle.
- No earlier damage to the vehicle is known.
- Nothing suggests the damage happened before the coverage started.
- The driver is named on the policy.
text:
Entry 1: The driver, who is named on the policy, reported a low-speed head-on collision in a parking area and a neck and back injury to the claimant. Coverage was active at the time, and nothing suggests the vehicle damage predates the policy start.

Entry 2: The attending officer recorded the claimant as present in the vehicle at the scene, but the file holds no separate report of the collision itself. No witnesses or photos have been identified so far.

Entry 3: The vehicle inspection shows dents to the front bumper cover and hood, positioned lower and toward the passenger side than the impact the driver described. The location and height do not line up with the account given.

Entry 4: The claimant describes the impact as a light bump but reports severe neck and back pain. The severity of the claimed injury is hard to square with a contact that seems this minor.

Entry 5: Prior medical history was checked, and there is no record of earlier injury to the neck or back. Nothing in the records points to a preexisting condition in that area.

Entry 6: On the follow-up call, the claimant repeated the same account of the collision, in the same order and with the same details as the first statement. No new facts came up.

Entry 7: Treatment began with an initial clinic visit, then moved to physiotherapy and medication. Visits gradually tapered as the claimant reported improvement, which is a usual course for a strain of this kind.

Entry 8: Records of prior claims and the vehicle's service history were reviewed, and no earlier damage to the vehicle is known.

Entry 9: Policy inception and endorsement dates were confirmed. Nothing suggests the damage occurred before coverage started.

Entry 10: The claimant has not been represented by counsel and has been asked for photos of the scene and any witness contact details. None have been provided at this stage.

Entry 11: The file was reviewed against the inspection findings and the treatment timeline. The gap between the reported impact and the damage pattern remains open for discussion with the handling team.

Entry 12: Claim remains open pending further review of the damage evaluation and the treatment records. The next step is to confirm the impact location with the repair shop before any decision is made.
